issues: All three quotes are verbatim on the Pew page (--check FOUND). The title details are correct: 5,101 U.S. adults, 15–21 May 2023, published 18 October 2023.

'Surveys show concern rising' overstates Pew's finding. Pew's chapter 1 says 'Similar sentiments were expressed in 2019, when we last asked about this.' The clear rise is in concern about government use: 64% to 71%, driven by Republicans (63% to 77%). Concern about company use moved only from 79% (2019) to 81% (2023), and Pew does not call that a change. The correction should say concern is holding steady or rising, and should give the 81% company figure so readers are not left thinking only government concern was measured.

fieldFixes.correction: Surveys show concern holding steady or rising, not falling: Pew found in 2023 that 81% of Americans are concerned about how companies use their data and 71% about government use (up from 64% in 2019), and that 67% say they understand little or nothing about what companies do with their data, up from 59% in 2019.

issues: All four quotes are verbatim (--check FOUND). The CCPA quote is §7025(b) of the regulations 'Effective 1/1/2026', page 44. The Texas quote is Bus. & Com. Code §541.055(e) as enrolled in HB 4. The GDPR quote is Art. 21(5), which the fetch shows opening 'In the context of the use of information society services, and notwithstanding Directive 2002/58/EC, the data subject may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications.'

Texas wording is imprecise and undated. The statute does not 'treat a browser setting as the consumer's authorised agent'. It says a consumer 'may designate an authorized agent using a technology, including ... an Internet browser setting or extension'. HB 4 §7(b) also states that §541.055(e) 'takes effect January 1, 2025', later than the rest of the Act (July 1, 2024). The statute further lets a controller decline a request it cannot verify.

The claim names Do Not Track, but the correction's US examples bind only qualifying opt-out signals such as Global Privacy Control. California §7025(b)(2) requires the signal to make clear it opts the consumer out of sale/sharing. The page cited for Colorado names Global Privacy Control as 'the state's first universal opt-out mechanism'. Do Not Track's legal force comes mainly through GDPR Art. 21(5): in 2023 the Berlin Regional Court (Landgericht Berlin, 16 O 420/19, not yet final when the ruling was reported) barred LinkedIn from telling users it ignores DNT signals. A vzbv source for this is appended, and the correction is reworded to match.
The final sentence about IEEE 7012 had no source on the record. The IEEE SA standard page is appended.

fieldFixes.correction: Not any more, in a growing number of places. California's regulations require businesses that sell or share personal information to process qualifying opt-out preference signals, such as Global Privacy Control, as valid opt-out requests. Colorado has required controllers to accept universal opt-out mechanisms since 1 July 2024. Since 1 January 2025, Texas has let consumers use a browser setting or extension to designate an authorised agent that opts them out. The GDPR has let people object 'by automated means' since 2018, and in 2023 a Berlin court barred LinkedIn from telling users it ignores Do Not Track signals. What these signals still cannot do is state positive terms, the gap IEEE 7012 (MyTerms) addresses.

sourceFixes.note: Re-fetched: FOUND verbatim as §7025(b), on page 44 of the PDF headed 'CALIFORNIA CONSUMER PRIVACY ACT REGULATIONS Effective 1/1/2026'. §7025(b)(1)–(2) sets the conditions: a commonly used format such as an HTTP header, and a clear disclosure that the signal opts the consumer out of sale/sharing.
